title: Economics · Episode 3
chapters: Why the Aussie dollar rises and falls
Smith, Marx, Keynes and Hayek: the great economic debate

units.t: Economics. Episode three.
In this episode: Why the Aussie dollar rises and falls, Recessions: when economies shrink and Smith, Marx, Keynes and Hayek: the great economic debate.
Part one. Why the Aussie dollar rises and falls.
In 2001 an Australian dollar bought less than 50 US cents.
A decade later it bought more than a US dollar.
Here is what moves a currency.
A price like any other.
When you hear that the Australian dollar is ‘at 65 US cents’, it means one Australian dollar can be swapped for 65 American cents.
An exchange rate is a price, and like other prices it is set by supply and demand.
Every day, importers, exporters, tourists, investors and banks buy and sell currencies.
Trading is enormous, measured in trillions of US dollars a day worldwide.
If more people want Australian dollars, perhaps to buy Australian iron ore or bonds, the price rises.
If more want to sell them, it falls.
The Australian dollar, nicknamed the Aussie, is one of the most heavily traded currencies in the world.
Floating the dollar.
It was not always this way.
For decades Australia's currency was pegged, first to the British pound, then to the US dollar, and from 1974 to a basket of currencies that officials adjusted.
The government and Reserve Bank effectively decided the rate, and strict controls limited how much money could flow in or out.
Defending the peg became harder as money sloshed around the world.
In December 1983 the Hawke government, with Treasurer Paul Keating, floated the dollar and removed most exchange controls, letting the market set the price.
Since then the Reserve Bank has only occasionally stepped into the market, usually during severe disorder.
What moves the Aussie.
Australia sells vast quantities of iron ore, coal, gas, gold, wheat and beef.
When those prices climb, foreign buyers need more Australian dollars, so the currency tends to rise.
That is why traders call it a commodity currency.
In the 2000s, China's industrialisation lifted the dollar from under 48 US cents in 2001 to above parity in late 2010, peaking in 2011.
When commodity prices later fell, so did the dollar.
Interest rates matter too.
If Australian rates exceed those in the United States or Japan, investors buy Australian dollars to earn more.
The carry trade borrows in a low-rate currency, such as the yen, to invest in a higher-rate one.
It can unwind suddenly, which is why the Aussie often falls in global crises.
Winners and losers.
Whether a high dollar is good news depends on who you are.
When the Aussie is strong, overseas holidays are cheaper, imported cars and electronics cost less, and Australians can buy foreign shares more cheaply.
But exporters suffer, because their goods become more expensive for foreign buyers, and local manufacturers struggle against cheaper imports.
Universities and tourism operators also feel it, since Australia becomes a pricier place to study or visit.
A weak dollar flips these effects.
Overseas trips hurt, but farmers, miners and tour operators gain.
This makes the exchange rate a kind of shock absorber for the economy, cushioning the blow when commodity prices or global conditions change.
The Big Mac test.
If a currency is fairly priced, the same basket of goods should cost roughly the same everywhere once you convert the money.
Economists call this idea purchasing power parity.
In 1986 The Economist magazine turned it into a light-hearted gauge called the Big Mac index.
If a Big Mac costs much more in Switzerland than in the United States after conversion, the Swiss franc looks overvalued by burger logic.
The index is deliberately simple, since local wages, rents and taxes all affect burger prices.
But it captures a real idea.
In the long run, exchange rates tend to drift towards levels that make prices broadly comparable, even if they stray widely in the short term.
The key idea: An exchange rate is simply the price of one currency in terms of another, set by supply and demand.
Part two. Recessions: when economies shrink.
Australia once went almost 30 years without one, a record for a rich country at the time.
What exactly is a recession, and what can governments do about it?
What is a recession.
A recession is a significant, widespread decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months.
In Australia, the media usually applies a rule of thumb: two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP, known as a 'technical recession'.
Economists prefer a broader view.
In the United States, a committee of the National Bureau of Economic Research dates recessions by weighing employment, incomes, spending and production together.
An economy can dip without a technical recession, and a sharp rise in unemployment can hurt more than GDP figures suggest.
A very deep, long recession is called a depression.
What triggers them.
Recessions usually start when spending drops sharply across the economy.

Common triggers include financial crises, when banks stop lending; central banks raising rates hard to fight inflation; supply shocks like the oil price spikes of the 1970s; the bursting of share or property bubbles; and wars or pandemics.
Once spending falls, a vicious circle can take hold.
Businesses sell less, so they cut staff and investment.
Newly unemployed people spend less, which hurts other businesses.
Fear spreads too: worried households save rather than spend, even if their own jobs are safe, deepening the downturn.
Two Australian slumps.
The Great Depression began around 1929, marked by the Wall Street crash that October, and lasted much of the 1930s.
World trade collapsed.
Australia, dependent on wool and wheat exports and overseas borrowing, was hit hard, with unemployment peaking at around 30% in 1932 by union estimates.
Devaluing the Australian pound in 1931 made exports cheaper for foreign buyers and gave farmers some relief, but recovery was slow.
The 1990-91 recession followed a late-1980s boom in borrowing, property and shares.
The RBA lifted rates sharply, with mortgage rates reaching about 17% in 1989.
Several banks and building societies ran into trouble, and unemployment rose to about 11% in 1992.
Paul Keating called it 'the recession we had to have'.
It locked in lower inflation, and the RBA adopted its inflation target in 1993.
Nearly three decades.
After 1991, Australia went nearly 29 years without a technical recession, the longest run of any advanced economy at the time.
Helping factors included floating the dollar in 1983, tariff cuts, an independent central bank, strong population growth and booming Chinese demand for minerals.
Critics note that population growth flattered the figures, since GDP per person fell in some periods.
In the 2008 global financial crisis, much of the world suffered its worst recession since the 1930s after Lehman Brothers collapsed.

Australia recorded one negative quarter but avoided a technical recession, thanks to a well-regulated banking system, rapid RBA rate cuts, a deposit guarantee, stimulus including cash payments of up to $900 and school building, and China's own massive stimulus.
How governments respond.
The pandemic ended the run.
Real GDP fell about 7% in the June quarter of 2020, the largest quarterly fall on record.
Unlike most recessions, it was caused deliberately by health measures.
JobKeeper paid employers $1,500 a fortnight per eligible worker, JobSeeker payments were temporarily boosted, and the RBA cut rates to 0.
The rebound was quick, though the stimulus is widely thought to have added to the inflation that followed.
Governments have two main tools: monetary policy, the RBA cutting rates, and fiscal policy, extra spending, tax cuts and payments.
Automatic stabilisers help too: when unemployment rises, welfare payments rise and tax revenue falls.
Households can keep an emergency fund of a few months' expenses, manage debt and maintain their skills.
For personal decisions, talk to a licensed financial adviser.
The key idea: A recession is a significant, widespread fall in economic activity, often measured as two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP.
Part three. Smith, Marx, Keynes and Hayek: the great economic debate.
Four thinkers shaped how the modern world argues about markets, governments and fairness.
Their ideas still echo in every budget and election.
Smith and specialisation.
In 1776 Adam Smith opened The Wealth of Nations with a pin factory.
One worker alone might make one pin a day, and certainly not twenty.
Ten workers splitting the job into specialised steps could make around 48,000.
Specialisation plus trade, he argued, was the engine of prosperity.
A butcher or baker feeds us out of self-interest, not kindness, and competition steers that self-interest towards serving others.
He used the phrase 'invisible hand' only once in the book.

Smith was no cheerleader for business: he distrusted merchants conspiring to raise prices, criticised monopolies, and backed public spending on defence, justice, infrastructure and some basic education.
He had also written The Theory of Moral Sentiments, 1759, on how sympathy underpins morality.
Marx on capitalism.
Decades later, Karl Marx looked at the same industrial world and saw crowded slums, long hours and child labour.

In The Communist Manifesto, 1848, with Friedrich Engels, and the first volume of Capital, 1867, he argued that capitalism rested on conflict between those who owned factories and those who worked in them.
Workers, he claimed, produced more value than they were paid, and owners kept the difference as profit.
He predicted repeated crises and eventual overthrow.
His ideas inspired socialist movements and later communist states, whose record of repression and economic failure has been heavily criticised.
Many historians still credit him with sharpening questions about power, inequality and economic change.
Keynes and demand.
In the Great Depression of the 1930s, mass unemployment lasted for years, and advice to wait for markets to correct themselves looked hopeless.
In The General Theory, 1936, John Maynard Keynes offered a different diagnosis: an economy can get stuck with too little total spending, or demand.
When households and businesses are frightened, they cut back.
That cuts other people's incomes and causes more cutbacks.
In such times, he said, governments should step in, spending more or cutting taxes to restart demand, even if it means borrowing.
He had earlier written the much quoted line 'In the long run we are all dead', a jab at those who said things would sort themselves out eventually.
Hayek and prices.
Keynes's great rival was the Austrian-born economist Friedrich Hayek.
In The Road to Serfdom, 1944, he warned that heavy government planning could gradually erode personal freedom.
His most influential idea came in a 1945 essay, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'.
Useful knowledge, Hayek pointed out, is scattered among millions of people.
A farmer knows the weather on her land, and a shopkeeper knows what customers want this week.
No central planner could gather it all.
Prices act like a vast communication system.
If tin becomes scarce, its price rises, and people everywhere economise on tin without needing to know why.
Markets, in this view, are a way of coordinating knowledge.
Swings and balance.
After the Second World War, Keynesian ideas shaped policy across much of the West, including Australia, with governments aiming for full employment.
The 1970s changed that.
Oil shocks helped trigger stagflation, high inflation combined with high unemployment, which many Keynesian models struggled to explain.
Milton Friedman, who argued that 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon', gained influence.
From the 1980s, many governments, Australia's included, floated currencies, deregulated finance and gave central banks the job of controlling inflation.
After 2008, Keynesian stimulus returned.
Today almost every developed economy is a mixed economy, and most political arguments are about the balance: how much to tax, spend and regulate, and how to share the gains from growth.
The key idea: Adam Smith argued that specialisation and trade create wealth, with self-interest kept in check by competition and rules.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is an exchange rate?
Answer. The price of one currency in another.
Question two. What is a 'technical recession'?
Answer. Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP.
Question three. What did Smith's pin factory example show?
Answer. Splitting a job into steps multiplies output.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
